lesson.title: Every Possible Case, Laid Out in Rows
lesson.summary: A truth table lists every combination of True and False inputs to a boolean expression alongside the resulting output, turning a claim about logic into something you can check exhaustively rather than argue about.
lesson.body:
A truth table is a simple but powerful tool: a grid that lists every possible combination of True and False values for a set of boolean variables, along with the resulting value of some expression built from them. Because Python's boolean type has exactly two values, True and False, a single variable has two possible states, two variables have four combinations, and in general n variables produce two to the power of n rows. This is why truth tables stay small and manageable for the two or three variable expressions that show up in everyday conditionals, but grow quickly for anything larger, which is part of why programmers reach for named intermediate variables instead of writing eight-row conditions inline.

Truth tables are how you verify a logical rule instead of just trusting it. Consider the expression A and (not B), used for something like "the light is on and the switch is not locked." There are four rows, one for every combination of A and B. When A is True and B is True, not B is False, so the and gives False. When A is True and B is False, not B is True, so the and gives True. When A is False and B is True, the result is False regardless of B, since anything anded with False is False. When A is False and B is False, the result is again False, for the same reason. Laid out as a table:

A=True,  B=True  -> False
A=True,  B=False -> True
A=False, B=True  -> False
A=False, B=False -> False

Only one row out of four produces True, which matches the plain-English meaning: the expression is true exactly when A holds and B does not.

Truth tables are also the proof technique behind De Morgan's laws. To confirm that not (A or B) really does equal (not A) and (not B) for every case, you build a four-row table computing both sides independently for each combination of A and B, and check that the two output columns match row by row. If they match on all four rows, the equivalence is proven for every possible input, not just the cases someone happened to test by hand, which is a stronger guarantee than checking a few examples.

The three basic operators each have their own well-known table shapes, worth memorizing because everything more complex is built from them. AND is true in exactly one of its four rows, the row where both inputs are True. OR is true in three of its four rows, every combination except both-False. NOT simply flips a single input, so its table has only two rows, True mapping to False and False mapping to True. Once those three small tables are second nature, you can build the table for any larger expression mechanically, one column at a time, by computing each subexpression from the columns already filled in, the same way you would trace through operator precedence.

In actual Python code, you rarely write out a truth table as a literal table, but the same values are living inside your program every time you combine booleans. Running print((True and False) or (not False)) will show you one row of some implicit truth table, and if you are ever unsure whether a compound condition behaves the way you intend, sketching its truth table on paper for two or three variables is often faster and more reliable than staring at the code and guessing. This habit becomes especially useful once you start writing conditional statements, since a badly reasoned boolean expression inside an if statement will make the program branch the wrong way, and a truth table is the most direct way to catch that before it happens.
